extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, cultural policymakers, and educated readers interested in architectural theory
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for producing and judging architecture focused on moral, social, pedagogical, and stylistic principles (Obedience, preservation, national stylistic unity, pedagogy, and social function). A Victorian-era treatise aimed at shaping practice and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of the dead / Preservation of historic buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: The dead have still their right in them: that which they labored for ... we have no right to obliterate. What other men gave their strength, and wealth, and life to accomplish, their right over does not pass away with their death; still less is the right to the use of what they have left vested in us only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not destroy buildings for present convenience; destruction by mobs is illegitimate ('for a mob it is, and must be always ... the people who destroy anything causelessly are a mob, and Architecture is always destroyed causelessly'). A fair building is necessarily worth the ground it stands upon and no cause is valid for its destruction. Respect and preserve ancient architecture as an inheritance for future generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture as embodiment of polity, life, history, and faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Every form of noble architecture is in some sort the embodiment of the Polity, Life, History, and Religious Faith of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or design buildings as expressions of national and social character; architecture should reflect and communicate civic, historical, and religious identities rather than being merely utilitarian or fashionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience as the crowning principle
rubrics_metrics.description: That principle ... to which Polity owes its stability, Life its happiness, Faith its acceptance, Creation its continuance,--Obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat obedience (submission to law, discipline, restraint) as a central architectural virtue: it lends stability, beauty, and moral standing to buildings and the societies that produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject false notions of Liberty; prefer disciplined law
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing [as absolute Liberty] in the universe ... if by liberty you mean chastisement of the passions, discipline of the intellect ... Call it by any name rather than this, but its best and truest is, Obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse 'liberty' with license. Where 'liberty' is used to justify caprice or rebellion against received forms, prefer the disciplined idea of obedience (restraint, lawful freedom) in architectural practice and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of laws correlates with dignity of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly in proportion to the majesty of things in the scale of being, is the completeness of their obedience to the laws that are set over them ... 'are its laws strait?' For their severity will probably be commensurate with the greatness of the numbers whose labor it concentrates or whose interest it concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the dignity of an architectural practice or occupation by how strict and exact its rules are; major arts (like architecture) demand stricter law and discipline because of their scale and social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: National stylistic unity and a universal school
rubrics_metrics.description: The architecture of a nation is great only when it is as universal and as established as its language; and when provincial differences of style are nothing more than so many dialects ... that no individual caprice shall dispense with, or materially vary, accepted types and customary decorations; and that from the cottage to the palace ... every member and feature ... shall be as commonly current, as frankly accepted, as its language or its coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek and enforce a widely taught, commonly accepted national system or school of architecture so that forms and decorations are comprehensible and consistent across classes and regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not demand novelty for novelty's sake; choose a style first
rubrics_metrics.description: A day never passes without our hearing our English architects called upon to be original, and to invent a new style ... We want no new style of architecture. Who wants a new style of painting or sculpture? But we want some style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize adoption and mastery of a coherent style rather than continual invention of new styles; having an agreed code of forms is more important than whether it is new or old.

rubrics_metrics.name: True originality arises within mastered styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality in expression does not depend on invention of new words ... A man who has the gift, will take up any style that is going, the style of his day, and will work in that, and be great in that ... those liberties will be like the liberties that a great speaker takes with the language ... inevitable, uncalculated, and brilliant consequences of an effort to express what the language ... could not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate originality by fluency and inventive use within an established style, not by breaking rules for their own sake; liberties should be natural consequences of mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy: begin with copyism and absolute accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When we begin to teach children writing, we force them to absolute copyism, and require absolute accuracy ... In the same way our architects would have to be taught to write the accepted style. We must first determine what buildings are to be considered Augustan ... their modes of construction and laws of proportion are to be studied with the most penetrating care; then the different forms and uses of their decorations are to be classed and catalogued ... admitting not so much as an alteration in the depth of a cavetto, or the breadth of a fillet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach architecture first by strict copying of authorised models and precise study of proportions and decorations; only after thorough mastery should variation be permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit measured license only after masterly command
rubrics_metrics.description: Then, when our sight is once accustomed to the grammatical forms and arrangements ... then, and not till then, a license might be permitted; and individual authority allowed to change or to add to the received forms, always within certain limits; the decorations, especially, might be made subjects of variable fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow individual innovation only after demonstrable competence in the established grammar of the style, and limit departures to controlled, intelligible variations (especially in decoration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing a national style (avoid vulgarization and infantility)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not so, however, when we take into consideration the far more important questions of the facility of adaptation to general purposes, and of the sympathy with which this or that style would be popularly regarded ... I cannot conceive any architect insane enough to project the vulgarization of Greek architecture. Neither can it be rationally questionable whether we should adopt early or late, original or derivative Gothic ... We are equally precluded from adopting styles essentially infantine or barbarous, however Herculean their infancy, or majestic their outlawry, such as our own Norman, or the Lombard Romanesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a style that adapts easily to common uses and enjoys popular sympathy; avoid vulgarizations of inappropriate styles and discard infantile or barbarous forms. Ruskin suggests as feasible choices: (1) Pisan Romanesque, (2) early Gothic of the Western Italian Republics up to Giotto, (3) Venetian Gothic in pure development, (4) the English earliest decorated Gothic (with French decorative elements cautiously borrowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience, Unity, Fellowship, and Order as essential aims
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some things which we not only want, but cannot do without; and which all the struggling and raving in the world ... will never enable us to do without: and these are Obedience, Unity, Fellowship, and Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these four qualities as non-negotiable goals of architectural practice and policy; without them, national art will remain dilettante and unprosperous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture as productive, meaningful national employment
rubrics_metrics.description: I think that all [the arts] will languish until that takes the lead ... our architecture will languish ... unless the first principle of common sense be manfully obeyed, and an universal system of form and workmanship be everywhere adopted and enforced ... Freed from the agitation ... the architect would find his whole understanding enlarged ... the first, perhaps the least, of them would be an increased sense of fellowship among ourselves ... Economy increased tenfold ... domestic comforts uninterfered with ... and all the symmetry and sightliness of our harmonized streets and public buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value architecture as a means of providing technical and intellectual employment, fostering civic fellowship, economy, and public beauty; public spending should prioritize building meaningful structures over less elevating forms of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer crafts that develop intellect and skill over frivolous occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is much dexterity of hand, patience, and ingenuity thus bestowed [on cutting facets upon jewels], which are simply burned out in the blaze of the tiara ... He would be far more healthily and happily sustained by being set to carve stone; certain qualities of his mind ... would develope themselves in the nobler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing employment, favor arts and trades (stone carving, building) that cultivate skill, imagination, and intellectual development rather than occupations that waste human faculties for trivial ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain balance: restraint must not overpower natural character
rubrics_metrics.description: Though restraint, utter and unrelaxing, can never be comely, this is not because it is in itself an evil, but only because, when too great, it overpowers the nature of the thing restrained ... The balance wherein consists the fairness of creation is between the laws of life and being in the things governed and the laws of general sway to which they are subjected; and the suspension or infringement of either kind of law, or, literally, disorder, is equivalent to, and synonymous with, disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply restraint and obedience but avoid excessive enforcement that crushes the inherent nature of the building or function; aim for a balanced interplay between inherent character and imposed law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture cannot be manufactured by mere experiments or fads
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall not manufacture art out of pottery and printed stuffs; we shall not reason out art by our philosophy; we shall not stumble upon art by our experiments, not create it by our fancies: I do not say that we can even build it out of brick and stone; but there is a chance for us in these, and there is none else;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject attempts to 'create' architecture by superficial fashions, philosophical theorizing, or random experiments; genuine architecture arises through disciplined practice in durable materials and shared forms.
